The Bangla calendar is similar to the Bengali calendar but was officially revised in Bangladesh in 1966 to match fixed Gregorian months for administrative purposes.

Based upon the ancient Coptic calendar, the Ethiopian calendar has 13 months (12 of 30 days, plus one of 5–6 days) and is about 7–8 years behind the Gregorian because it calculates Christ’s birth differently.

The Japanese calendar uses Gregorian months and days, but counts years by the "reign era" of the current emperor, replacing Western year counts with era names (e.g., Reiwa 6 instead of 2024). Era names change upon imperial succession (when a new emperor takes the throne).

The official calendar of Iran and Afghanistan, the Solar Hijri calendar counts years starting at the Islamic Hijra (622 CE) and beginning each year at the March equinox. It is considered more seasonally precise than the Gregorian calendar.

The official calendar of Iran and Afghanistan, the Solar Hijri calendar counts years starting at the Islamic Hijra (622 CE) and beginning each year at the March equinox. It is considered more seasonally precise than the Gregorian calendar.

Introduced in North Korea in 1997, the Juche calendar designates 1912 (birth of Kim Il Sung) as year 1. Otherwise, it follows Gregorian months and days.
The Minguo calendar was introduced in early Republican China and counts years starting in 1912 (founding of the Republic). Otherwise it follows Gregorian month/day structure.

The Hebrew calendar is a "lunisolar" calendar whose months follow lunar cycles, with leap months added to align with the solar year. The year count starts from a traditional Jewish creation year (3761 BCE), leading to a modern year currently in the 5780s.
